opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core of the case comes from looking at the really long run of economic history rather than just the last century or so. If you zoom out, growth hasn't been constant at 2%. For most of human history it was close to zero, then it crept up, and then around the Industrial Revolution it jumped to the rates we're used to now. Over that long sweep, growth has actually been accelerating, and the 2% era is a pretty recent and maybe somewhat unusual period.

The standard story for why growth accelerated historically goes something like this. New ideas and technologies are what drive sustained growth, and ideas come from people. When the economy produced more output, that supported a larger population, which meant more people generating ideas, which produced more technology, which produced more output. So you had a feedback loop, and that loop gives you not just exponential growth but super-exponential growth, where the growth rate itself keeps rising.

Then something interesting happened around the demographic transition. As people got richer, they started having fewer kids. So more output stopped translating into more people, and that broke the loop. Population growth flattened, and growth settled into this roughly steady 2% per year that economists now treat as the normal state of things.

The reason AI matters so much in this picture is that it could restore that feedback loop, but in a much tighter form. If AI systems can do the work humans do, including research, engineering, and inventing new technologies, then the "population" of minds producing ideas is no longer limited by human demographics. It's limited by how much compute you have. And compute is something you can produce with the output of the economy. So more output means more chips, which means more AI workers, which means more ideas and more production, which means more output. Unlike with human population, that loop can turn over really fast. You can copy a trained model instantly, and you don't have to wait twenty years for it to grow up and get educated.

So the argument isn't some exotic claim that AI is magic. It's that the thing that made growth accelerate before was a loop between output and the number of minds doing productive work, and AI could close that loop again, potentially much more tightly than it ever was historically. If you plug that into fairly standard growth models, you very naturally get growth rates of 20 or 30 percent a year or more, not 2 or 3.

Of course, there are real objections. There could be bottlenecks in the parts of the economy that are hard to automate, like physical tasks, regulatory approvals, or experiments that just take wall-clock time. There's the Baumol-style argument that the slowest sectors end up dominating. And you could have humans choosing to slow things down. I take those seriously. But I think the burden is genuinely on the people who expect 2% to continue to explain why it would, given that we'd be introducing something that removes the main constraint that seems to have capped growth for the last hundred years or so.

r001.rationale: The response says growth was near zero for most of human history, accelerated around the Industrial Revolution, and that the roughly 2% era is recent.

r002.rationale: It does not mention distrust of long-run historical economic estimates.

r003.rationale: It describes a feedback loop in which more output supports more people generating ideas, which leads to more technology and output.

r004.rationale: It argues that AI could expand idea production beyond human demographic limits, but does not say AI systems and robots could perform all work needed to reproduce themselves; it also acknowledges physical-task bottlenecks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to see it is to ask where the 2% comes from in the first place, because 2% is not some law of nature. If you look at the long sweep of history, growth rates have accelerated over time. For most of human history we were growing at a tiny fraction of a percent per year, then with agriculture it ticked up, then with the industrial revolution it jumped to something like the 2% we're used to now. So the thing that's actually been stable is not the growth rate, it's this pattern where growth rates have gone up as the economy has gotten bigger. And the standard story for why that happened is a feedback loop: more people means more ideas, more ideas means more output, more output can support more people, and so on. That loop got cut off in the last century or so because population growth decoupled from economic growth. Richer societies stopped having more kids. So we've been stuck in a regime where the number of brains doing research grows slowly, and that caps how fast the frontier can move.

The case for AI is basically that it reconnects that loop. If you can turn compute into something that functions like cognitive labor, then the number of "researchers" is no longer bounded by human population growth. It's bounded by how fast you can build chips and data centers, which is something you can accelerate with the output of the economy itself. So you get this situation where output funds more compute, more compute means more AI researchers, more AI researchers means faster technological progress, including progress in making chips and making AI, and that drives more output. That's exactly the kind of feedback that historically produced accelerating growth, and it's not obvious why it would stop at 2%.

Now, I want to be careful about what I'm actually claiming. I'm not saying I'm confident we'll see 20% or 30% growth. There are real reasons it might not happen. Maybe physical bottlenecks dominate, like you can have a trillion brilliant AI scientists but you still have to wait for the cement to cure and the regulatory approvals to come through. Maybe there's something about human cognition that's harder to replicate than it looks from today's systems. Maybe the ideas just get harder to find fast enough that it eats the gains. Those are all live possibilities. But what I'd push back on is the instinct to treat 2% as the default and to put the burden of proof entirely on the fast-growth side. When I look at the models economists actually use, and I plug in "labor is no longer a fixed input," the models themselves tend to say growth goes way up. The people saying it stays at 2% are usually relying on an intuition that the future looks like the recent past, and that intuition has a pretty bad track record over longer horizons.

So my honest position is something like: I think there's a serious chance, not a fringe chance, that this century sees growth rates that would look absurd by twentieth-century standards. And I think the people who dismiss that are mostly not engaging with the mechanism, they're just reacting to how weird the conclusion sounds.

r001.rationale: It says growth was tiny for most of history, rose with agriculture, and reached roughly 2% with the Industrial Revolution.

r002.rationale: It criticizes relying on the recent past as a guide, but does not identify distrust of long-run historical economic estimates.

r003.rationale: It describes a reinforcing loop in which more people generate more ideas and output, which can support more people.

r004.rationale: It argues AI could expand cognitive labor through compute, but does not say AI systems and robots could perform all work needed to reproduce themselves.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic case is that AI could change one of the main constraints on economic growth, which is the supply of human cognitive labor. Right now, if you want more scientists or engineers, you need people to get trained, and that takes a long time. You can’t just invest more money and have twice as many researchers next year.

With AI, you potentially can do something much closer to that. If you have a system that can do the work of a researcher, then buying more compute lets you run more copies of it. And if those AI researchers help develop better chips, better algorithms, or better ways of producing things, that makes it cheaper to expand the economy’s productive capacity further. So you get a feedback loop: more production supports more investment in AI, and more AI helps increase production and improve technology.

The important question is how much of that loop can actually be automated. If AI is very good at some tasks but progress still depends on a small number of humans doing other tasks, those humans can become the bottleneck. And even if you automate cognitive work broadly, you still have to build factories, generate electricity, run experiments, and so on. Those things take time.

So I wouldn’t say that faster growth follows automatically from having impressive AI. But I do think there’s a pretty fundamental reason to take it seriously. The historical growth rate isn’t a physical constant. If we can accumulate the capacity to do research and other cognitive work in the way we accumulate machinery, rather than waiting for new generations of people, that could support growth substantially faster than two percent a year.

r001.rationale: It says the historical growth rate is not a physical constant, but does not identify roughly 2% growth as the result of historical acceleration from slower rates.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention distrust of long-run historical economic estimates.

r003.rationale: It describes a feedback loop between AI, investment, and production, but not one between population size and technological innovation.

r004.rationale: It discusses AI doing cognitive work and expanding through more compute, but does not argue that AI systems and robots could perform all the work needed to reproduce themselves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic case is that AI could make the process of producing new ideas much more scalable. Historically, economic growth has depended a lot on technological progress, and technological progress depends on people doing research, inventing things, and figuring out better ways to organize production. We can invest in educating more people, but it takes a long time to grow and train a human researcher.

If you could instead run an AI system that does the work of a researcher or an engineer, then you could use more compute to get more of that work. And some of that work could go toward improving AI itself, or improving the chips and other infrastructure that you need to run it. So you get this feedback loop: better AI helps you produce better technology, which lets you run more and better AI, which speeds up technological progress further.

That doesn’t mean everything suddenly becomes easy to scale. You still have factories to build, experiments to run, energy to generate, and institutions that can move pretty slowly. The question is how binding those constraints are, and how much AI can help work around them. But I don’t see a strong reason to think that the roughly 2 percent growth we’re accustomed to is some fundamental ceiling. If we can reproduce and improve the cognitive labor that drives innovation, that seems like a potentially very large change in the growth process.

r001.rationale: It mentions familiar growth of roughly 2% and historical technological progress, but does not say that modern growth resulted from historical acceleration rather than a constant rate.

r002.rationale: It does not mention distrust of long-run historical economic estimates.

r003.rationale: It describes a feedback loop between AI and technological progress, not a feedback loop between population size and innovation.

r004.rationale: It discusses AI scaling cognitive work but does not argue that AI systems and robots could perform all work needed to reproduce themselves and thereby escape the constraints on human-driven growth.
